title_en: Mitsubishi Tanabe Pharma Corporation v. Patent Reexamination Board of the State Intellectual Property Office — administrative dispute over reexamination of rejected invention patent application
ruling_gist_en: For a chemical product invention, the use and/or effect of the product shall be completely disclosed. Even for a compound with a first-of-its-kind structure, at least one use shall be recorded. If a person skilled in the art cannot predict, based on the prior art, that the invention can achieve the said use and/or effect, the specification shall also record qualitative or quantitative experimental data sufficient to prove to a person skilled in the art that the technical solution of the invention can achieve the said use and/or the expected effect.

full_text_en:
Mitsubishi Tanabe Pharma Corporation v. Patent Reexamination Board of the State Intellectual Property Office — administrative dispute over rejection of invention patent application and review

【Ruling Summary】

For inventions of chemical products, the use and/or effects of the product shall be fully disclosed. Even for a compound with a pioneering structure, at least one use shall be described. If a person skilled in the art cannot, based on the prior art, predict that the invention can achieve the stated use and/or effects, the specification shall also include qualitative or quantitative experimental data sufficient to prove, for a person skilled in the art, that the technical solution of the invention can achieve the stated use and/or expected effects.

Administrative Ruling of the Supreme People's Court

(2015) Zhi Xing Zi No. 352

Re-petitioner (plaintiff at first instance, appellant at second instance): Mitsubishi Tanabe Pharma Corporation. Domicile: 3-2-10 Doshomachi, Chuo-ku, Osaka, Japan.

Legal representative: Masayuki Mitsuka, Chairman and General Manager of the Corporation.

Agent ad litem: Chen Wenping, lawyer of Beijing King & Wood Mallesons Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Huang Haibo, lawyer of Beijing King & Wood Mallesons Law Firm.

Respondent (defendant at first instance, appellee at second instance): Patent Reexamination Board of the State Intellectual Property Office. Domicile: Floors 10-12, Yingu Building, No. 9, North Fourth Ring West Road, Haidian District, Beijing, People's Republic of China.

Legal representative: Ge Shu, Deputy Director of the Board.

Agent ad litem: Yin Junting, Examiner of the Board.

Agent ad litem: Pan Jun, Examiner of the Board.

The re-petitioner, Mitsubishi Tanabe Pharma Corporation (hereinafter referred to as Tanabe Corporation), filed a petition for retrial with this Court against the administrative judgment (2013) Gao Xing Zhong Zi No. 2364 rendered by the Beijing High People's Court in the case of administrative dispute over rejection of invention patent application and review with the respondent, Patent Reexamination Board of the State Intellectual Property Office (hereinafter referred to as the Patent Reexamination Board). This Court lawfully formed a collegial panel to review this case, and the review has now concluded.

Grounds for retrial petition by Tanabe Corporation: (1) The Reexamination Decision No. 47530 (hereinafter referred to as the contested decision) made by the Patent Reexamination Board with respect to the invention patent application titled "Novel Compounds" with application number 200480022007.8 (hereinafter referred to as the present application) found that the compound of formula (I) claimed in the present application was insufficiently disclosed in the specification. The second instance judgment was wrong in maintaining the contested decision while correcting the above erroneous finding. The present application claims a compound of formula (I) or a pharmaceutically acceptable salt thereof. The contested decision and the first instance judgment found that the specification did not fully disclose the claimed invention on the ground that the specification of the present application did not contain experimental data proving that the compound of formula (I) has relevant biological activity and pharmaceutical use. The second instance judgment held that whether a new compound can achieve a certain therapeutic effect or specific use is not a technical problem to be solved or a technical effect to be achieved by the claims for a new compound and its preparation method. Even if the specification does not fully disclose experimental data or other information showing that the new compound can achieve a certain therapeutic effect or specific use, it cannot be concluded that the specification is insufficiently disclosed with respect to the above claims. Based on this, the second instance judgment found that, for the technical solution in claim 1 of the present application that merely involves the substance of the compound of formula (I) itself, it is wrong to require the specification to fully disclose whether the compound can achieve a certain therapeutic effect from the perspective of sufficient disclosure. Therefore, the second instance judgment actually found that the contested decision and the first instance judgment were erroneous in their findings of fact and/or application of law with respect to the technical solution of the compound of formula (I) itself. In this case, Tanabe Corporation, as the patent applicant, should have had the opportunity to amend the claims to retain a technical solution that does not have grounds for rejection. It is also a common practice in patent reexamination for a patent applicant to amend claims based on the reexamination opinion of the Patent Reexamination Board to overcome the grounds for rejection. However, the error in the contested decision caused Tanabe Corporation to lose the opportunity to overcome the grounds for rejection by amending the claims. Under such circumstances, the second instance court should have set aside the contested decision and restored Tanabe Corporation's opportunity to amend the claims. (2) The second instance judgment erred in finding that the technical solution of "pharmaceutically acceptable salts of the compound of formula (I)" in claim 1 of the present application was insufficiently disclosed. The second instance judgment held that, where the claims do not specifically define what specific pharmaceutical use is "pharmaceutically acceptable," a person skilled in the art would consider the specific pharmaceutical use of "pharmaceutically acceptable salts of the compound of formula (I)" to be the therapeutic effect claimed by the inventor in the specification of the present application, namely, having inhibitory activity against sodium-dependent glucose transporter (SGLT) and corresponding pharmaceutical use. The second instance judgment's above understanding of "pharmaceutically acceptable salts" is erroneous. The criterion for determining whether a salt is pharmaceutically acceptable in the art is that the salt-forming reagent does not interfere with normal metabolism or physiological processes, i.e., it is non-toxic. Therefore, the pharmaceutically acceptable nature of a salt does not mean that such salt can endow the compound with a certain pharmaceutical use or therapeutic effect. The technical solution of "pharmaceutically acceptable salts of the compound of formula (I)" in claim 1 of the present application is merely an extension based on "the compound of formula (I)" to their pharmaceutically acceptable salts, i.e., salts that are non-toxic to the body and do not interfere with normal metabolism or physiological processes. For compounds having acidic or basic functional groups in their chemical structure, salt formation can be achieved through conventional acid-base reactions. In the examination practice of invention patents in the field of chemical pharmaceuticals, it is generally considered that if a compound is sufficiently disclosed or can be supported by the specification, its salts in a general sense are also sufficiently disclosed or can be supported. The Patent Reexamination Board has never treated a compound and its pharmaceutically acceptable salts differently in matters concerning sufficiency of disclosure for compound inventions. Given that the second instance judgment found that the compound of formula (I) claimed in the present application had been sufficiently disclosed in the specification, it should have found that the pharmaceutically acceptable salts of the compound of formula (I) were also sufficiently disclosed. (3) With respect to the divisional application claiming a compound of formula (IA) (which is structurally very close to the compound of formula (I)) or a pharmaceutically acceptable salt thereof, the Patent Reexamination Board rendered Reexamination Decision No. 67557 (hereinafter referred to as Decision No. 67557) finding that the specification of that divisional application sufficiently disclosed the compound of formula (IA) and its pharmaceutically acceptable salts. This case should also find that the specification of the present application sufficiently disclosed the compound of formula (I) and its pharmaceutically acceptable salts. It should be noted that the fact that the divisional application was deemed to be withdrawn does not mean that the applicant agreed with the Patent Reexamination Board's opinion that the divisional application did not meet the requirements of inventiveness; the result is irrelevant to this case. In summary, the second instance judgment had unclear findings of fact and erroneous application of law. Request to set aside the contested decision and the first and second instance judgments.

Opinion submitted by the Patent Reexamination Board: (1) Claim 1 of the present application seeks protection for a compound of formula (I) or a pharmaceutically acceptable salt thereof. Since the specification of the present application failed to clearly and completely describe the pharmaceutically acceptable salts claimed in claim 1, which does not comply with Article 26(3) of the Patent Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the Patent Law), and Tanabe Corporation did not overcome this defect by amending the technical solutions of the claims or other means, it was not improper for the contested decision to reject all claims of the present application as a whole. (2) The divisional application addressed by Decision No. 67557 has a different specification from that of the present application, and the claimed compound is also different from that of the present application. Moreover, the key prior art relied upon in Decision No. 67557, i.e., patent document WO01/68660, did not appear in the proceedings of this case. Therefore, the relevant reasoning and conclusions of Decision No. 67557 are not applicable to this case. Furthermore, with respect to the divisional application addressed by Decision No. 67557, because the applicant did not respond to the Patent Reexamination Board's office action which, based on the Chinese counterpart patent application CN1418219A of WO01/68660 as a comparative document, raised an opinion that the claims did not meet the inventiveness requirements under the Patent Law, the divisional application has been deemed to be withdrawn.

This Court holds that the issues in dispute in this case are: 1. Whether sufficient disclosure of a new compound requires that the specification must describe and verify that it has at least one use or effect; 2. Whether the specification of the present application sufficiently discloses the technical solution claimed in claim 1; 3. The impact of Decision No. 67557 on this case.

With respect to Issue 1. The second instance judgment held: "With respect to claims for a new compound product and its preparation method, it cannot be concluded that the specification is insufficiently disclosed merely because the specification does not fully disclose experimental data showing that the new compound can achieve a certain therapeutic effect or specific use. Although it may be necessary to consider the therapeutic effect or specific use that the compound can achieve when determining inventiveness and industrial applicability, this is a different issue from sufficiency of disclosure, and they should be judged separately. Whether the lack of experimental data in the specification to support the therapeutic effect or specific use claimed by the inventor would result in lack of inventiveness or industrial applicability should be judged according to the relevant provisions of the law on inventiveness or industrial applicability." This Court holds: First, a patent right for an invention, as an industrial property right, must have value for industrial application. Inventions for which the technical significance is uncertain or which have no positive effect should not be protected. Second, whether a technical solution of an invention has value for industrial application should be judged based on the content disclosed in the specification and the state of the prior art. That is, the patent specification is key to determining whether an invention has been substantially completed and whether patent protection should be granted. Therefore, the specification should record technical information on whether the invention has industrial value and whether it has been substantially completed. Based on this, Section 3.1 "Sufficient Disclosure of Chemical Product Inventions" in Chapter 10 of Part II of the Guidelines for Patent Examination, titled "Certain Provisions on the Examination of Invention Patent Applications in the Chemical Field," provides: "If the claimed invention is a chemical product itself, the specification shall describe the identification, preparation, and use of the chemical product." "For chemical product inventions, the use and/or effects of the product shall be fully disclosed. Even for a compound with a pioneering structure, at least one use shall be described." "If a person skilled in the art cannot, based on the prior art, predict that the invention can achieve the stated use and/or effects, the specification shall also include qualitative or quantitative experimental data sufficient to prove, for a person skilled in the art, that the technical solution of the invention can achieve the stated use and/or expected effects." The above criteria for judging sufficient disclosure of chemical product inventions comply with Article 26(3) of the Patent Law of China and have been long followed in Chinese patent examination practice. Finally, for inventions in the chemical field, requiring disclosure of their use and effects is determined by the characteristics of inventions in this field. In most cases, whether a chemical invention can be implemented and what use or effect it has are often difficult to predict and must be confirmed through experimental results. Therefore, this Court holds that, where a person skilled in the art cannot, based on the prior art, predict that a new compound possesses the use and/or effects described in the specification, the patent application specification shall record qualitative or quantitative experimental data that can demonstrate that the compound can achieve the stated use and/or expected effects.

With respect to Issue 2. Claim 1 of the present application seeks protection for a compound of formula (I) or a pharmaceutically acceptable salt thereof. According to the description in the specification, the purpose of the present application is to provide compounds having inhibitory activity against sodium-dependent glucose transporter (SGLT). The SGLT inhibitors prevent and treat diabetes and diabetic complications such as diabetic retinopathy, diabetic neuropathy, diabetic nephropathy, and delayed wound healing by lowering blood glucose levels in diabetic patients. The specification of the present application records a large number of preparation examples of specific compounds of formula (I) in which a thienylmethyl group and a 1-β-D-glucopyranosyl group are attached to a benzene ring. However, the specification does not provide any inhibitory activity data of the compound of formula (I) against SGLT or data on its blood glucose-lowering effect. Nor does it provide any qualitative or quantitative data proving that the compound of formula (I) has the said biological activity and pharmaceutical use. It merely asserts in the Summary of the Invention that the compound of formula (I) has the above activity and related pharmaceutical use. Although Tanabe Corporation cited a number of prior art documents disclosing SGLT inhibitors, the compounds in those prior art documents differ structurally from the compound of formula (I) in certain aspects, such as the B-ring not being a thiophene ring, or the linking group being different, or the substitution site being different, etc. Therefore, it cannot be concluded from this that any compound in which the B-ring is a thiophene ring, Y is CH2, and the linking moiety between the A-ring and glucose is a single bond necessarily has SGLT inhibitory activity. Nor can it be concluded, based on several known SGLT inhibitors having certain structures, that a person skilled in the art would understand that compounds having the structure (with the A-ring-Y-B-ring structure) all have SGLT inhibitory activity and that the A-ring-Y-B-ring structure only affects stability and the degree of activity but does not cause the activity to be lost. In summary, a person skilled in the art would have difficulty concluding from the specification of the present application and the prior art that the compound of formula (I) and its pharmaceutically acceptable salts have the above activity and related pharmaceutical use. The second instance judgment, without considering the analysis of the prior art in the contested decision, made the following finding: "If claim 1 of the present application merely seeks protection for the substance of the compound of formula (I) itself, then from the perspective of sufficient disclosure of the specification, it is not necessary for the specification to fully disclose whether the compound can achieve a certain therapeutic effect." This finding does not comply with the relevant provisions and criteria for sufficient disclosure of chemical product inventions, and this Court corrects it.

Furthermore, "pharmaceutically acceptable salts" is a customary term used in patent documents in the chemical pharmaceutical field. Its original meaning does not indicate that the salt has a certain pharmaceutical use, nor does it mean that the claimed compound, without a corresponding pharmaceutical use limitation, does not need to possess corresponding pharmaceutical use. Rather, it indicates that, on the basis that the corresponding compound possesses pharmaceutical use, the salt formed retains the pharmaceutical use of the compound itself while being suitable for pharmaceutical application. If the compound itself is sufficiently disclosed in the specification, it is generally considered that the disclosure of its salts in a general sense is also sufficient. The second instance judgment's interpretation of "pharmaceutically acceptable salts" as "salts having pharmaceutical use" and its treatment of the compound of formula (I) as lacking pharmaceutical use, thereby treating the criteria for sufficient disclosure of the compound of formula (I) and its pharmaceutically acceptable salts differently, was erroneous, and this Court corrects it.

With respect to Issue 3. Although both the compound of formula (IA) claimed in the divisional application addressed by Decision No. 67557 and the compound of formula (I) claimed in the present application contain a

structure, the overall structures of the two are different. In the divisional application addressed by Decision No. 67557, the positions corresponding to the A-ring and B-ring of the compound of formula (I) in the present application are both benzene rings. In the compound disclosed in patent document WO01/68660 submitted by the requester for invalidation in Decision No. 67557, the positions corresponding to the A-ring and B-ring of the compound of formula (I) in the present application are also both benzene rings. The difference between the compound of formula (IA) and the compound disclosed in WO01/68660 lies only in the linking group between the glucose group and the A-ring phenyl group: the former is a nitrogen atom, and the latter is an oxygen atom. However, the differences between the compound of formula (I) of the present application and the compound of formula (IA) and the compound disclosed in WO01/68660 are reflected not only in the linking group between the glucose group and the A-ring phenyl group but also in the B-ring. In the compound of formula (I) of the present application, the B-ring is a thiophene ring rather than a benzene ring, and the thiophene ring itself has different physical and chemical properties from the benzene ring. Therefore, even if it could be concluded from Attachment 8 of Decision No. 67557 (C. W. THORNBER, Chem. Soc. Rev., 8, 563, 1979, 18 pages) that the linking group between the glucose group and the A-ring phenyl group being O, S, CH2, or NH does not change the activity of the overall compound, the activity of the compound formed after replacing the phenyl group of the B-ring with a thienyl group is difficult to predict. A person skilled in the art could not predict from the prior art that the compound of formula (I) of the present application would also have SGLT inhibitory activity. Therefore, the relevant findings of Decision No. 67557 cannot overturn the finding in the contested decision that the compound of formula (I) claimed in the present application and its pharmaceutically acceptable salts were not sufficiently disclosed in the specification.

In conclusion, the contested decision found facts clearly and applied the law correctly. Although some of the reasoning in the second instance judgment was erroneous, the result of the judgment was correct. The retrial petition of Tanabe Corporation does not meet the circumstances specified in Article 91 of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China. Pursuant to Article 74 of the Supreme People's Court's Interpretation on Several Issues Concerning the Implementation of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, it is ordered as follows:

The retrial petition of Mitsubishi Tanabe Pharma Corporation is dismissed.
